source.author: hor
source.text: quin et Prometheus et Pelopis parens dulci laborem decipitur sono nec curat Orion leones aut timidos agitare lyncas Eheu fugaces, Postume, Postume, labuntur anni nec pietas moram rugis et instanti senectae afferet indomitaeque morti, non, si trecenis quotquot eunt dies, amice, places illacrimabilem Plutona tauris, qui ter amplum Geryonen Tityonque tristi compescit unda, scilicet omnibus quicumque terrae munere vescimur enaviganda, sive reges sive inopes erimus coloni.
source.text_original: quin et Prometheus et Pelopis parens / dulci laborem decipitur sono / nec curat Orion leones / aut timidos agitare lyncas / Eheu fugaces, Postume, Postume, / labuntur anni nec pietas moram / rugis et instanti senectae / afferet indomitaeque morti, / non, si trecenis quotquot eunt dies, / amice, places illacrimabilem / Plutona tauris, qui ter amplum / Geryonen Tityonque tristi / compescit unda, scilicet omnibus / quicumque terrae munere vescimur / enaviganda, sive reges / sive inopes erimus coloni.
source.text_english: Indeed Prometheus and the father of Pelops are beguiled of their suffering by sweet song, and Orion cares no longer to drive leopards or timid lynxes. Alas, Postumus, Postumus, the fleeting years slip away, and piety will bring no delay to wrinkles and to advancing old age and to unconquerable death, no, not if each day as they go by, my friend, you should appease tearless Pluto with three hundred bulls, he who restrains thrice-vast Geryon and Tityos with the gloomy flood; for all of us who feed on the bounty of earth must sail across it, whether we shall be kings or poor peasants.
